mutations.original_excerpt: a pressure sore is not just one more skin wound. In the medical records of 19,520 hip-fracture surgeries, people who already had a pressure sore before surgery were about 20% more likely to die within 30 days, about 60% more likely to get deep vein thrombosis, about 40% more likely to get pneumonia, and about 40% more likely to be readmitted unplanned; among 324 hospitalized elderly people followed for a year and a half, those with pressure sores had about 50% higher risk of death. The three things you can do all have evidence: electric air mattresses cut new pressure sores by about 60% compared with ordinary hospital-bed mattresses; actually carrying out the turning (that trial used wearable sensors as reminders) cut them by about 70% compared with routine care; and do not leave the person lying face down for long — the face-down position produces more sores than lying on the back. As for "turn every two hours or every four," a review of 11 trials in 4,462 people concluded it is very uncertain — what matters is whether the turning actually happens, not the clock. Check the tailbone, heels, hips, and shoulder blades once a day; if you find redness that does not fade under pressure, broken skin, or darkening, get a nurse or doctor the same day.

9 studies, 7 countries, 8.32 million people: for every 0.1 increase in the vegetation index of greenery within 500 meters of your home, the probability of dying over the same period was about 4% lower. What was measured is the greenery around the home, not how often you visit a park, and people living in greener areas also tend to be wealthier and enjoy better air. So do not read this as "going to the park extends your life"; the usable part is to factor nearby green space into where you choose to live.
